[\[26\]](#s.-naeem-et-al.,-“machine-learning-based-usd/pkr-exchange-rate-forecasting-us--ing-sentiment-analysis-of-twitter-data,”-computers,-materials-&-continua/computers,-materials-&-continua-\(print\),-vol.-67,-no.-3,-pp.-3451–3461,-jan.-2021,-doi:-10.32604/cmc.2021.015872.) used sentiment analysis of Twitter data to forecast the USD/PKR exchange rate with machine learning. The study demonstrated that incorporating sentiment analysis could enhance prediction accuracy. The main disadvantage was the reliance on social media data, which can be noisy and may only sometimes reflect actual market conditions.

The following section will explore the Ensemble models, discussing their methodolo- gies, applications, and advantages in improving predictive accuracy in forex price forecasting.

4. **Ensemble**

The integration of multiple ML and DL models into an ensemble has shown promising results in financial forecasting. Ensemble models combine the strengths of different algorithms to enhance predictive performance and generalisability, addressing the limitations of individual models. Ji et al. [\[27\]](#y.-ji,-a.-w.-c.-liew,-and-l.-yang,-“a-novel-improved-particle-swarm-optimization-with-long-short-term-memory-hybrid-model-for-stock-indices-forecast,”-ieee-access,-vol.-9,) introduced a novel hybrid model combining Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO) with LSTM networks to forecast stock indices. The PSO algorithm optimises the LSTM hyperparameters, improving the model’s predictive capabilities. This hybrid approach lever- ages PSO’s efficiency in searching the solution space and LSTM’s ability to capture temporal dependencies in financial time series data. Their findings demonstrated that the PSO-LSTM model significantly outperforms traditional and standalone LSTM networks, indicating its po- tential for superior accuracy in stock market predictions.

Ghosh et al. [\[28\]](#p.-ghosh,-a.-neufeld,-and-j.-k.-sahoo,-“forecasting-directional-movements-of-stock-prices-for-intraday-trading-using-lstm-and-random-forests,”-finance-research-letters,-vol.-46,-p.-102280,-may-2022,-doi:-10.1016/j.frl.2021.102280.) investigate the effectiveness of using a hybrid model that combines LSTM networks and random forests for predicting the directional movements of stock prices in

intraday trading. The authors developed a model that leverages the sequential learning capabili- ties of LSTM networks to capture temporal dependencies in stock price data and the robustness of random forests to handle non-linear relationships and interactions between features. This hybrid approach aims to improve the accuracy and reliability of stock price direction predic- tions. The study found that the hybrid LSTM-random forest model outperformed traditional methods in predicting the direction of stock price movements. This improvement is attributed to the model’s ability to capture temporal patterns and complex feature interactions. The model is particularly suited for intraday trading, where accurate short-term predictions are crucial for profitable trading decisions.

Figure 5: The architecture of the proposed hybrid model by Moghaddam et al. [\[29\]](#a.-h.-moghaddam-and-s.-momtazi,-“image-processing-meets-time-series-analysis:-pre--dicting-forex-profitable-technical-pattern-positions,”-applied-soft-computing,-vol.-108,)

Moghaddam and Momtazi [\[29\]](#a.-h.-moghaddam-and-s.-momtazi,-“image-processing-meets-time-series-analysis:-pre--dicting-forex-profitable-technical-pattern-positions,”-applied-soft-computing,-vol.-108,) proposed a hybrid model that integrates image process- ing techniques with time series analysis to predict profitable technical pattern positions in the forex market. Their approach leverages the strengths of both CNNs and LSTM networks. The CNN analyses candlestick chart patterns, while the CNN-LSTM combination captures tempo- ral dependencies in the time series data. The architecture of this hybrid model is depicted in Figure [5\.](#figure-5:-the-architecture-of-the-proposed-hybrid-model-by-moghaddam-et-al.-[29]) In the model, raw data is preprocessed and then fed into two separate analysis paths. The candlestick analysis model uses CNN to extract features from the candlestick charts. Si- multaneously, the time series analysis model, which combines CNN and LSTM, processes the sequential data. Both model’s outputs are concatenated and passed through a dense layer fol- lowed by a dropout layer to prevent overfitting, ultimately providing the target predictions. This innovative approach demonstrates the potential of combining image processing with deep learning for enhanced predictive accuracy in financial markets.

Escudero et al. [\[18\]](#p.-escudero,-w.-alcocer,-and-j.-paredes,-“recurrent-neural-networks-and-arima-models-for-euro/dollar-exchange-rate-forecasting,”-applied-sciences,-vol.-11,-no.-12,-p.-5658,-jun.-2021,-doi:-10.3390/app11125658.) compared RNN and Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average

(ARIMA) models for forecasting the Euro/Dollar exchange rate. They developed a hybrid model integrating ARIMA for trend and seasonality detection with RNN to capture non-linear temporal dynamics. The combined ARIMA-RNN model exhibited enhanced predictive accu- racy over standalone models, suggesting its effectiveness in forex exchange rate forecasting. Wang and Guo [\[30\]](#y.-wang-and-y.-guo,-“forecasting-method-of-stock-market-volatility-in-time-series-data-based-on-mixed-model-of-arima-and-xgboost,”-china-communications,-vol.-17,-no.-3,) proposed a mixed model combining ARIMA and XGBoost to forecast stock market volatility. The ARIMA component captures linear trends, while XGBoost models the non-linear aspects of the time series data. Their hybrid approach demonstrated superior forecasting accuracy and robustness compared to traditional models, highlighting its potential for improved stock market volatility predictions.

Figure 6: CNN-LSTM network structure used by He et al. [\[4\]](#k.-he,-q.-yang,-l.-ji,-j.-pan,-and-y.-zou,-“financial-time-series-forecasting-with-the-deep-learning-ensemble-model,”-mathematics,-vol.-11,-no.-4,-p.-1054,-feb.-2023,-doi:-10.3390/math11041054.)

He et al. [\[4\]](#k.-he,-q.-yang,-l.-ji,-j.-pan,-and-y.-zou,-“financial-time-series-forecasting-with-the-deep-learning-ensemble-model,”-mathematics,-vol.-11,-no.-4,-p.-1054,-feb.-2023,-doi:-10.3390/math11041054.) propose a deep learning ensemble model for financial time series forecast- ing, integrating fundamental and technical data. The authors use a dataset comprising historical financial time series data, including forex pairs like EUR/USD and GBP/USD, sourced from financial databases and market data providers. The ensemble approach combines multiple deep- learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy and robustness. The study shows that the ensemble model outperforms individual models regarding prediction accuracy and generalisa- tion to various market conditions. The research validates the effectiveness of using ensemble strategies in financial forecasting by leveraging diverse data sources and model architectures. The network structure used by the authors involves a CNN-LSTM architecture shown in FIgure [6,](#figure-6:-cnn-lstm-network-structure-used-by-he-et-al.-[4]) where the CNN layers extract features from the input data, and the LSTM layers capture the temporal dependencies. This combination leverages the strengths of CNNs in handling spatial features and LSTMs in modeling sequential data, leading to improved forecasting performance. These studies underscore the advantages of using ensemble models in financial fore-

casting. By integrating the strengths of different algorithms, ensemble models can achieve higher accuracy and better generalisation than individual models.

5. **Related Research**

Forex prediction has seen extensive research efforts to improve the forecasting model’s accu- racy and reliability. These efforts span various methodologies, including technical analysis, fundamental analysis, and the integration of sentiment analysis. By utilising ML and DL tech- niques, researchers have aim to identify complex patterns and dependencies in financial data. This offers an overview of important related research, emphasising key studies that have ad- vanced forex prediction. The review covers works employing machine learning algorithms, deep learning models, ensemble methods, and hybrid approaches, illustrating the diverse strate- gies used to address the challenges in forex forecasting. The studies reviewed here highlight the importance of combining different analytical methods to enhance the predictive performance of forex models, reflecting the multi-faceted nature of financial markets.

Dautel et al. [\[3\]](#a.-j.-dautel,-w.-k.-ha¨rdle,-s.-lessmann,-and-h.-v.-seow,-“forex-exchange-rate-forecast--ing-using-deep-recurrent-neural-networks,”-digital-finance/digital-finance,-vol.-2,-no.-1–2,-pp.-69–96,-mar.-2020,-doi:-10.1007/s42521-020-00019-x.) explore the application of deep RNNs, such as LSTM networks and GRUs, for forecasting foreign exchange rates. The authors systematically compare these ad- vanced architectures with traditional recurrent and feedforward networks. The dataset includes historical forex data for major currency pairs like EUR/USD, GBP/USD, and USD/JPY, col- lected from reputable financial databases. The study finds that deep learning models, particu- larly LSTMs and GRUs, show superior directional forecasting accuracy and trading profitabil- ity performance. However, the authors note the challenges in implementing and tuning these complex architectures, suggesting that simpler neural networks can sometimes achieve compa- rable results. The research underscores the potential of deep learning in forex forecasting while acknowledging the practical difficulties in model deployment.

This paper by Ahmed et al. [\[6\]](#s.-ahmed,-s.-u.-hassan,-n.-r.-aljohani,-and-r.-nawaz,-“flf-lstm:-a-novel-prediction-system-using-forex-loss-function,”-applied-soft-computing,-vol.-97,-p.-106780,-dec.-2020,-doi:-10.1016/j.asoc.2020.106780.) introduces a novel prediction system called FLF-LSTM, which incorporates a specialised Forex Loss Function to improve the accuracy of Forex price predictions. The dataset includes historical forex data for pairs like EUR/USD, GBP/USD, and AUD/USD obtained from financial data providers. By integrating fundamental and technical indicators, the model leverages the strengths of LSTM networks in handling sequential data and capturing complex temporal dependencies. The Forex Loss Function is designed to enhance the model’s sensitivity to forex market dynamics, resulting in improved predictive performance compared to traditional loss functions.

Qi et al. [\[21\]](#l.-qi,-m.-khushi,-and-j.-poon,-“event-driven-lstm-for-forex-price-prediction,”-2020-ieee-asia-pacific-conference-on-computer-science-and-data-engineering-\(csde\),-dec.-2020,-doi:-10.1109/csde50874.2020.9411540.) present an Event-Driven LSTM model for forex price prediction that in- corporates external market-moving events into the forecasting process. The dataset includes historical forex price data for pairs such as EUR/USD and USD/JPY and event data like eco- nomic announcements and geopolitical developments sourced from financial news outlets and economic calendars. By integrating these event data into the LSTM framework, the model en- hances its ability to predict forex price movements. The study demonstrates that considering

external events dramatically improves the prediction accuracy of LSTM models, highlighting the importance of incorporating diverse data sources in financial forecasting.

Sudimanto et al. [\[8\]](#sudimanto,-y.-heryadi,-lukas-and-a.-wibowo,-”foreign-exchange-prediction-using-ma--chine-learning-approach:-a-pilot-study,”-2021-4th-international-conference-on-infor--mation-and-communications-technology-\(icoiact\),-yogyakarta,-indonesia,-2021,-pp.-239-242,-doi:-10.1109/icoiact53268.2021.9563998) conducted a pilot study demonstrating the effectiveness of machine learning algorithms in predicting exchange rates. Their study employed machine learning tech- niques to forecast forex prices, including SVM and random forests. The findings indicated that these models could significantly enhance prediction accuracy compared to conventional methods.

research conducted by Vuong et al. The study leverages the strengths of XGBoost in handling structured data and the sequential learning capabilities of LSTM networks. The results show that the hybrid XGBoost-LSTM model outperforms the individual model’s prediction accuracy and robustness. However, one of the main limitations is the increased complexity and computational cost associated with combining two different machine learning models, which requires careful parameter tuning and significant computational resources.

Islam and Hossain [\[33\]](#islam-and-e.-hossain,-“foreign-exchange-currency-rate-prediction-using-a-gru--lstm-hybrid-network,”-soft-computing-letters,-vol.-3,-p.-100009,-dec.-2021,-doi:-10.1016/j.socl.2020.100009.) propose a hybrid network combining GRU and LSTM networks for predicting foreign exchange currency rates. The study aims to leverage the strengths of both GRU and LSTM in capturing temporal dependencies and non-linear patterns in the data. The CNN component extracts features from the input data, while the TLSTM network captures temporal dependencies. The study demonstrates that the CNN-TLSTM model outperforms traditional and standalone deep learning models in terms of predictive accuracy. The main limitation of the CNN-TLSTM model is its complexity and the computational resources required for training, which necessitates extensive hyperparameter tuning and careful selection of input features.

Tripathi et al. The paper by Peng and Lee [\[37\]](#y.-l.-peng-and-w.-p.-lee,-“data-selection-to-avoid-overfitting-for-foreign-exchange-intra--day-trading-with-machine-learning,”-applied-soft-computing,-vol.-108,-p.-107461,-sep.-2021,-doi:-10.1016/j.asoc.2021.107461.) focuses on mitigating overfitting in forex trading mod- els. The paper by Dassanayake [\[38\]](#w.-dassanayake,-“critical-comparison-of-statistical-and-deep-learning-models-applied-to-the-new-zealand-stock-market-index.,”-2022) provides an in-depth analysis of different forecasting models. The study highlights the strengths and weaknesses of each approach, showing that deep learning models, especially those designed to capture tem- poral dependencies, outperform statistical models in terms of accuracy and handling market volatility. The research uses historical stock market data from New Zealand to validate the models, underscoring the practical applications of advanced forecasting techniques in financial markets.

A survey conducted by Hu et al. [\[42\]](#m.-ulina,-r.-purba,-and-a.-halim,-“foreign-exchange-prediction-using-ceemdan-and-improved-fa-lstm,”-2020-fifth-international-conference-on-informatics-and-comput--ing-\(icic\),-nov.-2020,-doi:-10.1109/icic50835.2020.9288615.) explores the use of Complementary Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition with Adaptive Noise (CEEMDAN) and an Improved Fractional-Order Adaptive LSTM (FA-LSTM) model for forex prediction. [\[46\]](#d.-p.-neghab,-m.-cevik,-m.-i.-m.-wahab,-and-a.-basar,-“explaining-exchange-rate-fore--casts-with-macroeconomic-fundamentals-using-interpretive-machine-learning,”-compu--tational-economics,-may-2024,-doi:-10.1007/s10614-024-10617-1.) investigated using machine learning models to explain exchange rate forecasts with macroeconomic fundamentals. The study applied interpretive machine learning techniques to a dataset comprising key macroeconomic indicators from significant economies. Figure 8: Proposed methodology by Adegboye and Kampouridis [\[47\].](#a.-adegboye-and-m.-kampouridis,-“machine-learning-classification-and-regression-mod--els-for-predicting-directional-changes-trend-reversal-in-fx-markets,”-expert-systems-with-applications,-vol.-173,-p.-114645,-jul.-2021,-doi:-10.1016/j.eswa.2021.114645.)

Figure [8](#figure-8:-proposed-methodology-by-adegboye-and-kampouridis-[47].) describes the proposed methodology used by Adegboye and Kampouridis for their forex prediction model. The methodology is divided into two main phases: training and testing. The physical time dataset is first input into a symbolic regression genetic program- ming (GP) model in the training phase. This model generates a symbolic regression model

(B) and determines the directional change (DC) threshold (A). The physical time dataset is

also transformed into a DC dataset (C). AutoWeka is then employed to optimize the param- eters and select the best classification model. The physical time dataset is again transformed into a DC dataset in the testing phase. This dataset is fed into the optimized classification model. The model predicts whether the end of an overshoot (OS) event or a DC event has been reached. Based on these predictions, a proposed trading strategy is developed, guiding trading decisions. Adegboye and Kampouridis [\[47\]](#a.-adegboye-and-m.-kampouridis,-“machine-learning-classification-and-regression-mod--els-for-predicting-directional-changes-trend-reversal-in-fx-markets,”-expert-systems-with-applications,-vol.-173,-p.-114645,-jul.-2021,-doi:-10.1016/j.eswa.2021.114645.) examined various machine learning mod- els, including classification and regression techniques, to predict directional changes and trend reversals in forex markets. Filippou et al. [\[48\]](#i.-filippou,-m.-p.-taylor,-and-z.-wang,-“media-sentiment-and-currency-rever--sals,”-journal-of-financial-and-quantitative-analysis,-pp.-1–47,-jun.-2023,-doi:-10.1017/s0022109023000534.) analysed the impact of media sentiment on currency reversals. The study utilised sentiment analysis on a vast corpus of financial news articles and correlated the sentiment scores with currency exchange rate movements. The results indicated that neg- ative media sentiment often preceded currency reversals, suggesting that integrating sentiment analysis into forex prediction models can improve their accuracy and responsiveness to market events.

Semiromi et al. Song and Choi [\[52\]](#h.-song-and-h.-choi,-“forecasting-stock-market-indices-using-the-recurrent-neural-net--work-based-hybrid-models:-cnn-lstm,-gru-cnn,-and-ensemble-models,”-applied-sciences,-vol.-13,-no.-7,-p.-4644,-apr.-2023,-doi:-10.3390/app13074644.) compared various hybrid models for forecasting stock market indices, including CNN-LSTM, GRU-CNN, and ensemble models. [\[53\]](#i.-e.-livieris,-e.-pintelas,-and-p.-pintelas,-“a-cnn–lstm-model-for-gold-price-time--series-forecasting,”-neural-computing-&-applications,-vol.-32,-no.-23,-pp.-17351–17360,-apr.-2020,-doi:-10.1007/s00521-020-04867-x.) proposed a CNN-LSTM model for forecasting gold prices. The study utilised historical gold price data and validated the model’s effectiveness in forecasting financial time series. Paliari et al. casting. This study highlights the advan- tages of using advanced machine learning techniques over traditional statistical models for time series forecasting. Pornwattanavichai et al. [\[55\]](#a.-pornwattanavichai,-s.-maneeroj-and-s.-boonsiri,-”bertforex:-cascading-model-for-forex-market-forecasting-using-fundamental-and-technical-indicator-data-based-on-bert,”-in-ieee-access,-vol.-10,-pp.-23425-23437,-2022,-doi:-10.1109/ac--cess.2022.3152152.) introduced BERTFOREX, a cascading model for forex market forecasting that integrates fundamental and technical indicators using the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) framework. The results demonstrate that the deep learning approach significantly out- performs traditional methods regarding predictive accuracy. However, the high computational cost associated with processing and training on large volumes of order book data remains a notable limitation, which may only be feasible for some trading environments.

Weerathunga and Silva [\[58\]](#h.-p.-s.-d.-weerathunga-and-a.-t.-p.-silva,-”drnn-arima-approach-to-short-term-trend-forecasting-in-forex-market,”-2018-18th-international-conference-on-advances-in-ict-for-emerging-regions-\(icter\),-colombo,-sri-lanka,-2018,-pp.-287-293,-doi:-10.1109/icter.2018.8615580.) introduce a hybrid DRNN-ARIMA approach for short- term trend forecasting in the forex market. The model combines DRNN with the ARIMA model to enhance short-term prediction accuracy. Leveraging the strengths of both methods, the hybrid model shows improved forecasting performance. Despite these advantages, the model’s complexity and the need for extensive parameter tuning are significant drawbacks, making

it time-consuming and computationally expensive. Mate´ [\[59\]](#c.-g.-mate´,-“forecasting-in-forex-the-spot-price-interval-of-tomorrow-with-the-same-information-of-today.-an-analysis-of-the-seven-majors-using-a-linear-regression-model-based-on-interval-arithmetic,”-knowledge-based-systems,-vol.-258,-p.-109923,-dec.-2022,-doi:-10.1016/j.knosys.2022.109923.) investigates forecasting forex

spot price intervals using a linear regression model based on interval arithmetic. This study analyses seven major currency pairs and employs interval arithmetic to predict price ranges for the following day. Although the approach offers a unique perspective on interval prediction, its main limitation lies in the simplistic linear regression model, which may not effectively capture the complexities and non-linear relationships inherent in forex data. Talebi et al. [\[60\]](#h.-talebi,-w.-hoang,-and-m.-l.-gavrilova,-“multi-scale-foreign-exchange-rates-ensemble-for-classification-of-trends-in-forex-market,”-procedia-computer-science,-vol.-29,-pp.-2065–2075,-jan.-2014,-doi:-10.1016/j.procs.2014.05.190.) present a multi-scale ensemble model designed for classifying trends in the forex market. The model combines predictions from multiple scales to improve trend classification accuracy. Findings indicate that the multi-scale ensemble approach enhances predictive performance compared to single-scale models. Nevertheless, the increased computational complexity and the challenge of integrating multiple scales effectively are significant limitations.

Panda et al. [\[61\]](#m.-m.-panda,-s.-n.-panda-and-p.-k.-pattnaik,-”exchange-rate-prediction-using-ann-and-deep-learning-methodologies:-a-systematic-review,”-2020-indo-–-taiwan-2nd-interna--tional-conference-on-computing,-analytics-and-networks-\(indo-taiwan-ican\),-rajpura,-india,-2020,-pp.-86-90,-doi:-10.1109/indo-taiwanican48429.2020.9181351.) conduct a systematic review of exchange rate prediction using ANN and deep learning methodologies. This review highlights various ANN and deep learning mod- els applied to forex prediction, discussing their advantages and limitations. A significant limi- tation noted is the overfitting problem commonly encountered in deep learning models, which can negatively impact their generalisability to new data. Juszczuk and Krus´ [\[62\]](#p.-juszczuk-and-l.-krus´,-“soft-multicriteria-computing-supporting-decisions-on-the-forex-market,”-applied-soft-computing,-vol.-96,-p.-106654,-nov.-2020,-doi:-10.1016/j.asoc.2020.106654.) develop a soft multicriteria computing approach to support decision-making in the forex market. Their model integrates multiple criteria to improve decision-making accuracy. While the approach is innovative, its primary limitation is the complexity of accurately weighting and integrating multiple criteria, which can be subjective and challenging to implement effectively. Rundo [\[63\]](#f.-rundo,-“deep-lstm-with-reinforcement-learning-layer-for-financial-trend-predic--tion-in-fx-high-frequency-trading-systems,”-applied-sciences,-vol.-9,-no.-20,-p.-4460,-oct.-2019,-doi:-10.3390/app9204460.) investigates the integration of a deep LSTM with a reinforcement learning layer for financial trend prediction in high-frequency trading systems. The model combines the sequence mod- eling capabilities of LSTM with reinforcement learning to enhance predictive accuracy and decision-making. Despite the promising results, the computational intensity and the need for substantial data to train the reinforcement learning component are significant challenges.

6. **Summary**

This subsection summarises the problems and challenges identified in the reviewed literature, explaining the selection of XGBoost, LSTM, Transformer, and ensemble models for this re- search.

* **Problems and Challenges in ML Models:**

  * Sudimanto et al. [\[8\]](#sudimanto,-y.-heryadi,-lukas-and-a.-wibowo,-”foreign-exchange-prediction-using-ma--chine-learning-approach:-a-pilot-study,”-2021-4th-international-conference-on-infor--mation-and-communications-technology-\(icoiact\),-yogyakarta,-indonesia,-2021,-pp.-239-242,-doi:-10.1109/icoiact53268.2021.9563998) highlighted the complexity and computational intensity of ML models like SVM and random forests, which limit their efficiency in financial forecasting.

  * McNally et al. [\[9\]](#s.-mcnally,-j.-roche-and-s.-caton,-”predicting-the-price-of-bitcoin-using-ma--chine-learning,”-2018-26th-euromicro-international-conference-on-parallel,-dis--tributed-and-network-based-processing-\(pdp\),-cambridge,-uk,-2018,-pp.-339-343,-doi:-10.1109/pdp2018.2018.00) noted issues of overfitting and the extensive parameter tuning required for ML models, reducing robustness in volatile market conditions.

  * Basak et al. [\[10\]](#suryoday-basak,-saibal-kar,-snehanshu-saha,-luckyson-khaidem,-sudeepa-roy-dey,predicting-the-direction-of-stock-market-prices-using-tree-based-classifiers,-the-north-american-journal-of-economics-and-finance,volume-47,2019,pages-552-567,issn-1062--9408,https://doi.org/10.1016/j.najef.2018.06.013.) discussed the sensitivity of tree-based classifiers to noisy data and their tendency to overfit in highly volatile markets.

  * Thu and Xuan [\[11\]](#t.-n.-t.-thu-and-v.-d.-xuan,-”using-support-vector-machine-in-forex-predicting,”-2018-ieee-international-conference-on-innovative-research-and-development-\(icird\),-bangkok,-thailand,-2018,-pp.-1-5,-doi:-10.1109/icird.2018.8376303.) emphasised the computational expense and complexity of opti- mising SVMs, making them less practical for frequent prediction updates.

  * Neghab et al. [\[12\]](#d.-p.-neghab,-m.-cevik,-m.-i.-m.-wahab,-and-a.-basar,-“explaining-exchange-rate-fore--casts-with-macroeconomic-fundamentals-using-interpretive-machine-learning,”-computa--tional-economics,-may-2024,-doi:-10.1007/s10614-024-10617-1.) highlighted the reliance on accurate and timely macroeconomic data, which can cause delays in prediction updates.

* **Selection of XGBoost:**

  * XGBoost models deliver promising results due to their ability to handle large datasets and capture complex patterns effectively [\[8\].](#sudimanto,-y.-heryadi,-lukas-and-a.-wibowo,-”foreign-exchange-prediction-using-ma--chine-learning-approach:-a-pilot-study,”-2021-4th-international-conference-on-infor--mation-and-communications-technology-\(icoiact\),-yogyakarta,-indonesia,-2021,-pp.-239-242,-doi:-10.1109/icoiact53268.2021.9563998)

  * They offer robust performance by integrating technical, fundamental, and sentiment data for comprehensive market analysis.

* **Problems and Challenges in DL Models:**

  * Ni et al. [\[31\]](#l.-ni,-y.-li,-x.-wang,-j.-zhang,-j.-yu,-and-c.-qi,-“forecasting-of-forex-time-series-data-based-on-deep-learning,”-procedia-computer-science,-vol.-147,-pp.-647–652,-jan.-2019,-doi:-10.1016/j.procs.2019.01.189.) found that LSTM models outperform traditional statistical models but require extensive hyperparameter tuning and significant computational resources.

  * Vuong et al. [\[32\]](#p.-h.-vuong,-t.-t.-dat,-t.-k.-mai,-p.-h.-uyen,-and-p.-bao,-“stock-price-forecasting-based-on-xgboost-and-lstm,”-computer-systems-science-and-engineering,-vol.-40,-no.-1,) highlighted the increased complexity and computational cost of combining models like XGBoost and LSTM.

  * Islam and Hossain [\[33\]](#islam-and-e.-hossain,-“foreign-exchange-currency-rate-prediction-using-a-gru--lstm-hybrid-network,”-soft-computing-letters,-vol.-3,-p.-100009,-dec.-2021,-doi:-10.1016/j.socl.2020.100009.) discussed the increased training time and computational complexity due to combining GRU and LSTM models.

  * Wang et al. [\[34\]](#j.-wang,-x.-wang,-j.-li,-and-h.-wang,-“a-prediction-model-of-cnn-tlstm-for-usd/cny-exchange-rate-prediction,”-ieee-access,-vol.-9,-pp.-73346–73354,-jan.-2021,-doi:-10.1109/access.2021.3080459.) demonstrated that CNN-TLSTM models outperform traditional models but require substantial computational resources for training.

* **Selection of LSTM and Transformer Models:**

  * LSTM models excel in capturing long-term dependencies and temporal patterns, providing better predictive accuracy for financial time series [\[31\].](#l.-ni,-y.-li,-x.-wang,-j.-zhang,-j.-yu,-and-c.-qi,-“forecasting-of-forex-time-series-data-based-on-deep-learning,”-procedia-computer-science,-vol.-147,-pp.-647–652,-jan.-2019,-doi:-10.1016/j.procs.2019.01.189.)

  * Transformer models are effective in handling longer sequences and capturing com- plex patterns, making them promising for financial applications [\[22\].](#p.-bilokon-and-y.-qiu,-“transformers-versus-lstms-for-electronic-trading,”-social-sci--ence-research-network,-jan.-2023,-doi:-10.2139/ssrn.4577922.)

* **Advantages of Ensemble Models:**

  * Ensemble models combine the strengths of various algorithms to enhance predictive performance and generalisability, addressing the limitations of individual models

  * Ghosh et al. [\[28\]](#p.-ghosh,-a.-neufeld,-and-j.-k.-sahoo,-“forecasting-directional-movements-of-stock-prices-for-intraday-trading-using-lstm-and-random-forests,”-finance-research-letters,-vol.-46,-p.-102280,-may-2022,-doi:-10.1016/j.frl.2021.102280.) showed that hybrid models combining LSTM networks and ran- dom forests improve the accuracy and reliability of stock price direction predictions.

  * He et al. [\[4\]](#k.-he,-q.-yang,-l.-ji,-j.-pan,-and-y.-zou,-“financial-time-series-forecasting-with-the-deep-learning-ensemble-model,”-mathematics,-vol.-11,-no.-4,-p.-1054,-feb.-2023,-doi:-10.3390/math11041054.) validated the effectiveness of using ensemble strategies in financial forecasting by leveraging diverse data sources and model architectures.

* **Combining LSTM and XGBoost:**

  * LSTM and XGBoost models were combined in this research to leverage their com- plementary strengths in time-series forecasting. LSTM is well-suited for capturing long-term temporal dependencies in sequential data, while XGBoost is effective in modeling non-linear relationships and feature interactions within structured data.

  * The novelty of this approach lies in using LSTM to model long-term trends in forex data and XGBoost to capture short-term fluctuations by integrating technical, fun- damental, and sentiment indicators.

  * By combining these models, the research addresses limitations of existing approaches where single models either focus solely on time-series patterns (LSTM) or feature- based prediction (XGBoost). This hybrid model enhances predictive accuracy by capturing both sequential dependencies and complex relationships between fea- tures.

  * This research also stands out by applying the hybrid model to multiple currency pairs and two different time intervals (four-hour and one-day), making the approach more robust and generalizable across different market conditions.

* **Identified Gaps in the Literature:**

  * While significant progress has been made in applying ML and DL models to fi- nancial forecasting, the integration of sentiment analysis with technical and funda- mental indicators remains underexplored. Most studies focus solely on technical indicators, overlooking the potential benefits of using multiple data sources for im- proving prediction accuracy.

  * Many of the existing studies, such as Ghosh et al. [\[28\],](#p.-ghosh,-a.-neufeld,-and-j.-k.-sahoo,-“forecasting-directional-movements-of-stock-prices-for-intraday-trading-using-lstm-and-random-forests,”-finance-research-letters,-vol.-46,-p.-102280,-may-2022,-doi:-10.1016/j.frl.2021.102280.) focus on a single currency pair, limiting the generalisability of their findings. This research expands on previ- ous work by using multiple currency pairs and two different time intervals, thereby providing a broader and more comprehensive analysis of forex market prediction.

  * Few studies systematically compare the performance of ML, DL, and hybrid en- semble models in forex prediction using diverse data types. This leaves a gap in understanding which models offer the best predictive accuracy and robustness in financial markets.

* **Conclusion:**

  * The challenges and gaps identified in the literature support the selection of XG- Boost, LSTM, Transformer, and ensemble models in this research. By addressing the limitations of traditional ML and DL models and focusing on the integration of diverse data sources, including multiple currency pairs and time intervals, this study aims to enhance the predictive accuracy and robustness of forex price forecasts.

3. **Methodology**

This chapter outlines the comprehensive methodologies employed to investigate forex price predictions utilising a multi-modal approach that integrates technical indicators, fundamental analysis, and sentiment analysis derived from financial news. It meticulously describes the data collection process, detailing the types and sources used, including historical forex rates, economic indicators, and sentiment data. Furthermore, it elaborates on the model development process, illustrating the deployment of various advanced machine learning and deep learning models tailored to analyse and predict forex market movements. Additionally, this section specifies the evaluation metrics used to assess the models’ accuracy and efficacy, ensuring the research findings’ validity and reliability. Through a clear exposition of these methods, this chapter aims to provide a robust framework supporting replicability and scrutiny of the research outcomes.

1. **Data Collection**

The data collection phase of this research forms the foundation upon which the predictive mod- els are built, encompassing a diverse array of datasets to ensure a comprehensive analysis of forex market dynamics. This section delineates the methodologies employed to gather and prepare three distinct types of data: sentiment analysis data, technical trading data, and fun- damental economic indicators. Each data type uniquely contributes to the model’s ability to predict forex price movements, providing a multifaceted view of the factors influencing cur- rency values. The sources from which data was collected, the criteria for its selection, and the processes involved in its preparation are detailed, aiming to furnish a robust dataset that supports the sophisticated analytical techniques used in this study.

Significantly, two different timeframes of market data were utilised to capture varying market dynamics: One-Day OHLC data, and Four-Hour OHLC data. The Four-hour data was paired explicitly with sentiment analysis data and technical and fundamental indicators, aiming to capture the immediate impact of market sentiment on forex prices within shorter intervals. This combination was mainly selected to assess the influence of rapidly changing market sentiments alongside economic and technical indicators, providing a detailed temporal resolution suitable for high-frequency trading strategies.

Conversely, the One-Day OHLC data was used exclusively with technical and funda- mental indicators. This broader timeframe allowed for examining longer-term trends and eco- nomic impacts without the immediate noise of market sentiment, offering insights into the more stable, underlying movements in forex prices. This strategic differentiation in data utilisation enabled a comparative analysis of model performance across four key forex pairs (EUR/USD, NZD/USD, EUR/NZD, and AUD/NZD) under different architectural setups for each dataset. This approach highlights each model configuration’s relative strengths and weaknesses and

showcases how different data integrations can impact predictive accuracy in forex market pre- diction.

1. **Sentiment Analysis**

Sentiment analysis is crucial in understanding market trends and predicting forex price move- ments. This section details the methodology employed to collect and process sentiment data from financial news headlines, highlighting the tools and techniques used to ensure a compre- hensive and accurate dataset.

Figure 9: The Sentiment Analysis Workflow for Forex News Headlines.

Advanced web scraping tools and libraries were utilised to collect sentiment data. Se- lenium, an automation tool that simulates user interactions with web pages, was essential for navigating dynamic content. BeautifulSoup, a Python library for parsing HTML and XML doc- uments, was used to extract specific elements such as news headlines and publication [dates\[64\],](#g.-fatouros,-j.-soldatos,-k.-kouroumali,-g.-makridis,-and-d.-kyriazis,-“transforming-sentiment-analysis-in-the-financial-domain-with-chatgpt,”-machine-learning-with-applications,-vol.-14,-p.-100508,-dec.-2023,-doi:-10.1016/j.mlwa.2023.100508.) [\[65\].](#c.-m.-liapis,-a.-karanikola,-and-s.-kotsiantis,-“a-multi-method-survey-on-the-use-of-sentiment-analysis-in-multivariate-financial-time-series-forecasting,”-entropy,-vol.-23,-no.-12,-p.-1603,-nov.-2021,-doi:-10.3390/e23121603.) Pandas, a data manipulation and analysis library, organised and stored the extracted data in structured formats. These tools were chosen for their robustness and ability to handle com- plex web scraping tasks, ensuring the reliability and comprehensiveness of the collected data.

The sentiment data was sourced from three prominent financial news websites, each known for its extensive coverage of forex-related news. Investing.com is a widely used platform that offers real-time data, news, and analysis on financial markets. It is popular among traders and investors for its comprehensive coverage of market trends and events [\[66\].](#investing.com,-“forex-and-currency-news,”-available-at) This platform provided a substantial portion of the sentiment data used in this study.

DailyForex.com focuses on forex news, analysis, and educational content. It offers in-depth market insights and trading strategies, making it a valuable resource for novice and experienced traders [\[67\].](#dailyforex,-“currency-exchange-rates---currency-trading-rates-—-dailyforex.com,”-available-at-https://www.dailyforex.com/currencies.) The site’s detailed analysis and up-to-date information on market movements contributed significantly to the sentiment data collected for this research.

Interest.co.nz is a New Zealand-based financial news website covering various eco- nomic and market topics. It provides localised news and analysis on the NZD currency, offering unique insights into the New Zealand forex market [\[68\].](#interest.co.nz,-“currencies,”-available-at-https://www.interest.co.nz/currencies.) This site was beneficial for gathering sentiment data related to the NZD currency pairs.

From these sources, a total of 2048 news headlines were collected over the period from January 1, 2023, to January 31, 2024\. The distribution of headlines among the different forex pairs was as follows: EUR/NZD with 246 headlines, NZD/USD with 585 headlines, EUR/USD with 466 headlines, and AUD/NZD with 192 headlines. This diverse data set from multiple rep- utable sources ensured a comprehensive analysis of market sentiment, improving the robustness of the predictive models.

The process involved several steps. First, web scraping with Selenium automated the opening of web pages and waited for dynamic content to load, which is crucial for handling websites with JavaScript-driven content. BeautifulSoup then parsed the HTML content of the web pages and extracted necessary elements, such as news titles and publication dates, ensuring only relevant information was captured. After collecting data from each website, the datasets were combined into a single comprehensive dataset using Pandas, ensuring consistency in the data format.

Once collected, the news headlines were processed using state-of-the-art Large Lan- guage Models (LLMs): GPT-4, and GEMINI Advanced. GPT-4, utilised for its advanced zero- shot learning capabilities, interprets context-rich financial news without explicit prior training on financial sentiment. GEMINI Advanced, designed for complex narrative understanding, provides deep insights from financial texts even without labeled data. Each headline was as- signed a sentiment score (positive, neutral, or negative) based on the output of these models.  
![][image25]

Figure 10: Heatmap showing Spearman correlation coefficients for EUR/USD data.

The sentiment classification process involved assigning scores of 1 for positive senti- ment, 0 for neutral sentiment, and \-1 for negative sentiment to each headline. These daily senti- ment scores were aggregated to derive a comprehensive sentiment analysis score for each day. Given that the primary dataset operates on a Fourhour timeframe, Figure [10](#figure-10:-heatmap-showing-spearman-correlation-coefficients-for-eur/usd-data.) shows the ROC 9 indicator—which represents the rate of change over a one-and-a-half-day period—provides a meaningful way to correlate the aggregated daily sentiment scores with forex price movements. This methodology allows for a nuanced understanding of how daily market sentiment influ- ences price trends over subsequent days, capturing the temporal dynamics between sentiment shifts and their market effects. The comprehensive sentiment analysis process is illustrated in Figure [9,](#figure-9:-the-sentiment-analysis-workflow-for-forex-news-headlines.) which outlines the sequential steps from web scraping to data extraction, sentiment classification, and sentiment score aggregation. This structured approach ensures that the sen- timent data collected is relevant, timely, and accurately reflects market conditions, providing a solid foundation for subsequent predictive modeling.For the sentiment analysis, the following zero-shot prompt was used: *”Provide a sentiment analysis for the following headlines regard- ing the specified currency pair. Indicate whether each headline is positive, negative, or neutral for the specified currency pair.”* This approach enabled us to effectively categorise the head- lines without the need for pre-labeled data, leveraging the advanced capabilities of the LLMs [\[69\],](#s.-a.-farimani,-m.-v.-jahan,-a.-m.-fard,-and-s.-r.-k.-tabbakh,-“investigating-the-informativeness-of-technical-indicators-and-news-sentiment-in-financial-mar--ket-price-prediction,”-knowledge-based-systems,-vol.-247,-p.-108742,-jul.-2022,-doi:-10.1016/j.knosys.2022.108742.) [\[70\].](#c.-i.-lee,-c.-chang,-and-f.-n.-hwang,-“currency-exchange-rate-prediction-with-long-short-term-memory-networks-based-on-attention-and-news-sentiment-analysis,”-2019-international-conference-on-technologies-and-applications-of-artificial-intelligence-\(taai\),-nov.-2019,-doi:-10.1109/taai48200.2019.8959884.) As shown in Figure [10,](#figure-10:-heatmap-showing-spearman-correlation-coefficients-for-eur/usd-data.) the Spearman correlation heatmap indicates that the GPT-4 sentiment score has a higher correlation with the close price compared to other sentiment mod- els. Therefore, for the EUR/USD pair, the GPT-4 sentiment analysis score is used for model training to enhance the predictive accuracy of the EUR/USD models.  
Following these steps, a robust dataset of financial news headlines was prepared for

sentiment analysis, offering valuable insights into market sentiment and its impact on forex price movements. This comprehensive approach ensures that the sentiment analysis component is grounded in a well-curated and diverse dataset, enhancing the overall reliability and accuracy of the predictive [models\[71\].](#w.-souma,-i.-vodenska,-and-h.-aoyama,-“enhanced-news-sentiment-analysis-using-deep-learning-methods,”-journal-of-computational-social-science,-vol.-2,-no.-1,-pp.-33–46,-jan.-2019,-doi:-10.1007/s42001-019-00035-x.)

2. **Technical Analysis**

Technical analysis is critical in forex market prediction, as it utilises historical price data and statistical indicators to forecast future price movements. This section delves into the various types of technical indicators used in this research, the rationale behind their selection, and the formulas used for their calculation. The primary indicators included in the dataset are derived from the Open, High, Low, and Close (OHLC) prices, calculated using the TA-Lib library, a comprehensive library for technical analysis [\[72,](#tradingview,-“comprehensive-financial-charts-for-analysis,”-available-at) [73\].](#ta-lib,-“technical-analysis-library,”-available-at-https://ta-lib.org/,-accessed-september-28,-2023.)

Open, High, Low, and Close (OHLC) Prices: OHLC prices form the foundational data from which various technical indicators are computed. Each of these prices represents different aspects of market behavior within a specific timeframe, providing a granular view of price action:

* **Open Price**: The price at which the forex pair begins trading at the start of a given period.

  * **High Price**: The maximum price reached during the trading period.

    * **Low Price**: The minimum price reached during the trading period.

      * **Close Price**: The price at which trading ends for the period.

**Average True Range (ATR):** ATR measures market volatility by considering the range of price movements. It is calculated based on the greatest of the following: the current high minus the current low, the absolute value of the current high minus the previous close, and the absolute value of the current low minus the previous close. The formula is presented below (Eq. [1):](#atr-=-1)

*ATR* \= 1

*i*\=1

Here, True Range is the maximum of (Eq. [2):](#true-range-=-max\(high-−-low,-|high-−-closeprev|,-|low-−-closeprev|\)-\(2\))

True Range \= max(High *−* Low*, |*High *−* Closeprev*|, |*Low *−* Closeprev*|*)	(2)

**Rate of Change (ROC):** ROC is a momentum oscillator that measures the percentage change in price between the current price and a price *n* periods ago. It indicates the speed at which the price is changing, which helps in identifying overbought or oversold conditions (Eq. [3):](#rocn-=-close-−-closen-periods-ago-×-100-\(3\)-closen-periods-ago)

*ROCn* \= Close *−* Close*n* periods ago *×* 100	(3) Close*n* periods ago

* **ROC 7**: Used in the One-day timeframe, it calculates the rate of change over seven days.

  * **ROC 9**: Used in the Four-hour timeframe, it calculates the rate of change over 36 hours (nine Four-hour periods).

**Relative Strength Index (RSI):** RSI is a momentum oscillator that measures the speed and change of price movements. It oscillates between 0 and 100 and is typically used to identify overbought or oversold conditions. The formula is presented below (Eq. [4):](#rsi-=-100-−-100)

where:

*RSI* \= 100 *−*  100

*RS* \= Average Gain over n periods Average Loss over n periods

* **RSI 14**: Calculated using 14 days, it helps understand the momentum of price changes and potential reversal points.

**Exponential Moving Average (EMA):** EMA is a moving average with greater weight and significance on the most recent data points. It reacts more quickly to recent price changes than the simple moving average (SMA). The formula is given in (Eq. [6):](#emat-=-α-×-pricet-+\(1-−α\)-×-emat−1-\(6\))

*EMAt* \= *α ×* Price*t* \+(1 *−α*) *×* EMA*t−*1	(6)

where:

* **EMA 50**: A 50-period EMA that smooths out price data to identify the trend direction over a medium-term period.

**Bollinger Bands:** Bollinger Bands consist of a middle band (usually a 20-period SMA) and two outer bands (upper and lower), standard deviations from the middle band. They measure market volatility and identify potential overbought or oversold conditions. The formulas are shown below (Eq. [8,](#middle-band-=-ma20-\(8\)) [9,](#upper-band-=-ma20-+\(2-×-standard-deviation20\)-\(9\)) [10):](#lower-band-=-ma20-−-\(2-×-standard-deviation20\)-\(10\))

Middle Band \= *MA*20	(8)

Upper Band \= *MA*20 \+(2 *×* Standard Deviation20)	(9)

Lower Band \= *MA*20 *−* (2 *×* Standard Deviation20)	(10)

**Selection of Technical Indicators**

The selection of the above technical indicators is rooted in their proven effectiveness in capturing various aspects of market behavior:

* ATR (Eq. [1\)](#atr-=-1) is essential for understanding market volatility, helping traders adjust their strategies based on the extent of price movements.

  * ROC indicators (ROC 7 and ROC 9\) (Eq. [3\)](#rocn-=-close-−-closen-periods-ago-×-100-\(3\)-closen-periods-ago) are crucial for identifying the momentum of price changes over different timeframes, which is critical for short-term and medium- term trading strategies.

    * RSI (Eq. [4\)](#rsi-=-100-−-100) provides insights into the momentum and potential reversal points, which are critical for timing entries and exits in the market.

      * EMA (Eq. [6\)](#emat-=-α-×-pricet-+\(1-−α\)-×-emat−1-\(6\)) helps smooth out price data to identify trends more accurately, reducing the noise from random price fluctuations.

      * Bollinger Bands (Eq. [8,](#middle-band-=-ma20-\(8\)) [9,](#upper-band-=-ma20-+\(2-×-standard-deviation20\)-\(9\)) [10\)](#lower-band-=-ma20-−-\(2-×-standard-deviation20\)-\(10\)) are invaluable for assessing market volatility and identi- fying overbought or oversold conditions, which can signal potential reversals.

These indicators offer a comprehensive view of market dynamics, enabling a nuanced analysis of price movements. By integrating these technical indicators, the models developed in this research aim to leverage the strengths of each indicator to enhance the accuracy of

forex price predictions. The combination of these indicators provides a robust framework for understanding and forecasting market behaviour across different timeframes, as detailed in subsequent sections of this research.

3. **Fundamental Analysis**

As the previous section shows, technical analysis indicators provide a robust framework for understanding market dynamics based on historical price data. This section focuses on fun- damental analysis, which complements technical analysis by incorporating economic and fi- nancial indicators that reflect the broader economic environment. Fundamental indicators offer deeper insights into the factors influencing currency values, providing a comprehensive under- standing of market movements. This section details the fundamental indicators used in this research, explaining their significance and impact on forex trading.

**Gold (GOLD CLOSE)**: Gold prices are often considered a safe-haven asset, meaning they tend to hold or increase in value during economic uncertainty. Investors flock to gold during fi- nancial instability, leading to price increases. Rising gold prices indicate a lack of confidence in fiat currencies, as gold is seen as a more stable store of value. This can impact forex pairs such as EUR/USD and NZD/USD, as movements in gold prices reflect broader economic sentiments that can influence currency valuations.

**US Dollar Index (DXY CLOSE)**: The US Dollar Index (DXY) measures the value of the USD against a basket of foreign currencies, including the euro, Japanese yen, British pound, Canadian dollar, Swedish krona, and Swiss franc. Movements in the DXY can have significant implications for currency pairs involving the USD. A rising DXY indicates a strengthening USD, which can affect the EUR/USD and NZD/USD pairs by making the USD more valuable relative to these currencies.

**Oil (OIL CLOSE)**: Oil prices influence many aspects of the global economy, including in- flation and trade balances. Countries that are major oil exporters or importers are particularly affected by fluctuations in oil prices. For example, higher oil prices can increase inflationary pressures in oil-importing countries, impacting their currency value. Conversely, oil-exporting countries may see their currency strengthen with rising oil prices. Therefore, oil price move- ments can affect forex pairs like EUR/USD and NZD/USD.

**S\&P 500 (S\&P CLOSE)**: The S\&P 500 is a broad measure of the US stock market’s perfor- mance and is an essential indicator of US economic health. A strong S\&P 500 typically signals a robust economy, which can strengthen the USD. Consequently, currency pairs tied to the USD, such as EUR/USD and NZD/USD, are influenced by the performance of the S\&P 500\. **Euro 50 (EU50 CLOSE)**: The Euro Stoxx 50 Index represents 50 of the Eurozone’s most extensive and most liquid stocks. It serves as a critical indicator for the EUR, reflecting the Eurozone’s economic health and investor sentiment. Movements in the Euro Stoxx 50 can impact pairs like EUR/USD and EUR/NZD, as changes in the index reflect shifts in economic stability and investor confidence.

**NZX 50 (NZX50 CLOSE)**: The NZX 50 Index includes the top 50 companies listed on the New Zealand Stock Exchange, serving as a barometer for the New Zealand economy. The performance of the NZX 50 affects the NZD, influencing currency pairs such as NZD/USD and EUR/NZD. A strong NZX 50 indicates economic growth and investor confidence in New Zealand, leading to a stronger NZD.

**ASX 200 (ASX200 CLOSE)**: The ASX 200 Index is a benchmark for the Australian equity market. It provides insights into the Australian economy, influencing the AUD. The perfor- mance of the ASX 200 affects the AUD/NZD pair, as it reflects Australia’s economic conditions and investor sentiment.

**Money Supply (M2 and M3)**: Money supply measures like M2 and M3 reflect the liquid- ity in the economy. M2 includes cash, checking deposits, and easily convertible near money, while M3 includes M2 plus large-time deposits, institutional money market funds, and other more considerable liquid assets. Changes in money supply can influence inflation and eco- nomic growth. For instance: EU M2 and US M2: These indicators reflect the Eurozone and US money supply, impacting EUR/USD. An increasing money supply can lead to inflationary pressures, affecting currency value. NZD M3 and AUD M3: These measures are crucial for understanding monetary conditions in New Zealand and Australia, influencing NZD/USD and AUD/NZD pairs.

**Inflation Rates (EUR, USD, NZD, AU)**: Inflation rates indicate the rate at which the general price level of goods and services rises, eroding purchasing power. High inflation typically leads to higher interest rates as central banks try to control inflation, affecting currency value. For example: EUR Inflation Rate: Understanding Eurozone inflation is vital for predicting EUR movements. High inflation may lead to higher interest rates, strengthening the EUR. USD Inflation Rate: US inflation impacts the USD’s value against the NZD in the NZD/USD pair. NZD and AU Inflation Rates: These rates affect the NZD and AUD, influencing pairs like NZD/USD and AUD/NZD. Central New Zealand and Australian banks may adjust interest rates in response to inflation, impacting currency value.

**Interest Rates (EUR, USD, NZD, AU)**: Central banks use interest rates to control inflation and stabilise the currency. Changes in interest rates impact currency value by affecting investment flows. Higher interest rates attract foreign investment, strengthening the currency. For instance: EUR and USD Interest Rates: These rates affect the EUR/USD pair. Higher Eurozone or US interest rates can attract investment, strengthening the EUR or USD. NZD Interest Rates: Influence the NZD/USD pair. Higher interest rates in New Zealand can attract investment, strengthening the NZD. AU Interest Rates: Affect the AUD/NZD pair. Changes in Australian interest rates influence the AUD, impacting the pair.

**Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**: GDP measures a country’s economic performance. Higher GDP growth typically strengthens a currency by signaling economic stability and growth. For example: US GDP and EUR/USD: US economic performance influences the USD. Strong GDP growth in the US can strengthen the USD, affecting the EUR/USD pair. NZ GDP and NZD/USD: New Zealand’s economic health affects the NZD. Strong GDP growth in New Zealand can strengthen the NZD, impacting the pair. EU GDP and EUR/USD: Eurozone eco- nomic performance impacts the EUR. Strong GDP growth in the Eurozone can strengthen the EUR, affecting the EUR/USD pair. AU GDP and AUD/NZD: Australia’s GDP influences the AUD. Strong GDP growth in Australia can strengthen the AUD, impacting the AUD/NZD pair. **Unemployment Rates (EUUR, USUR, NZUR, AUUR)**: Unemployment rates indicate eco- nomic health. Lower unemployment generally strengthens a currency by signaling economic stability. For example: US Unemployment Rate (USUR): Affects the USD in EUR/USD and NZD/USD pairs. Lower unemployment in the US can strengthen the USD. EU Unemployment Rate (EUUR): Impacts the EUR in EUR/USD and EUR/NZD pairs. Lower unemployment in the Eurozone can strengthen the EUR. NZ Unemployment Rate (NZUR): Influences the NZD in NZD/USD and EUR/NZD pairs. Lower unemployment in New Zealand can strengthen the NZD. AU Unemployment Rate (AUUR): Affects the AUD in AUD/NZD pairs. Lower unem- ployment in Australia can strengthen the AUD.

**Balance of Trade (BOT)**: The balance of trade (BOT) is the difference between a country’s exports and imports. A positive BOT (trade surplus) typically strengthens the currency, while a negative BOT (trade deficit) can weaken it. For example: USBOAT and EURBOT: Reflect trade balances for the US and Eurozone, impacting EUR/USD. A trade surplus in the US or

Eurozone can strengthen the USD or EUR. USBOT and NZBOT: Influence the USD and NZD in NZD/USD. A US or New Zealand trade surplus can strengthen the USD or NZD. AUBOT: Affects the AUD in AUD/NZD. A trade surplus in Australia can strengthen the AUD.

**Trade Indicators (NZGDTPI and NZTA)**: Specific to New Zealand, these indicators reflect trade terms and agreements, influencing the NZD. For example: NZGDTPI: The Global Dairy Trade Price Index affects the NZD in NZD/USD. Changes in dairy prices can influence New Zealand’s export revenues, impacting the NZD. NZTA: New Zealand Tourist Arrivals impact the NZD in NZD/USD and EUR/NZD. Tourist arrivals can affect trade flows and economic stability, influencing the NZD.

These fundamental indicators comprehensively overview the economic factors influ- encing forex markets. The research aims to leverage the broader economic context to enhance forex price prediction accuracy by integrating these indicators into predictive models. The combination of technical and fundamental analysis offers a holistic approach to understanding and forecasting market movements.

2. **Model Development**

In the previous section, we discussed the detailed data collection process, encompassing senti- ment analysis and technical and fundamental indicators. This comprehensive dataset forms the backbone of our research, providing the essential inputs needed for accurate forex price pre- diction. In this section, we will delve into the detailed structure of the five models employed in this study, illustrating how each model integrates the diverse data types to analyse and predict forex market movements. The models include LSTM, XGBoost, Transformer architectures, and Ensemble Models.

1. **LSTM**

The LSTM networks were employed to leverage their strength in capturing temporal patterns and dependencies in sequential data. The LSTM models were used with both One-day and Four-hour OHLC data, combined with technical indicators (TM), fundamental indicators (FM), and sentiment analysis (SA) scores. To ensure the data was suitable for LSTM input, prepro- cessing steps included standardizing the features and targets. The StandardScaler from the sklearn library was utilised for this purpose. Standardising the data ensured that all features had a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one, which is crucial for achieving stable and efficient training of the LSTM model. The data was structured into sequences using a time step, aligning with the chosen temporal resolution for the LSTM model. This involved creating sliding windows of data to capture the temporal dependencies effectively. Each window con- sisted of consecutive time steps of input features, with the target being the forex price at the subsequent time step.

The LSTM model was constructed using the TensorFlow Keras library. The archi- tecture included two LSTM layers with Dropout and BatchNormalisation layers to improve generalisation and model stability. The first LSTM layer was followed by a Dropout layer and a BatchNormalisation layer. The second LSTM layer was followed by another Dropout layer and another BatchNormalisation layer. The final output layer was a Dense layer with a single unit, representing the predicted forex price. L2 regularisation was applied to all lay- ers to prevent overfitting, which penalises large weights and encourages the model to learn simpler patterns. The Adam optimiser was employed with an initial learning rate. Adam is an adaptive learning rate optimisation algorithm well-suited for training deep learning mod- els. Learning rate scheduling was also implemented using the ReduceLROnPlateau callback, which reduces the learning rate when the validation loss plateaued, ensuring that the model continued learning even when improvements slowed. Early stopping was also employed using the EarlyStopping callback, which monitored the validation loss and stopped training if there was no improvement for a specified number of epochs, restoring the best weights observed during training. The model was trained for up to many epochs with a moderate batch size. The training process included validation data to monitor the model’s performance and prevent over- fitting. The ReduceLROnPlateau and EarlyStopping callbacks ensured efficient training by dynamically adjusting the learning rate and preventing overfitting.  
LSTM with Technical Indicators (LSTM TM): This configuration utilises technical in- dicators derived from One-day OHLC data to predict forex prices. The technical indicators included are ATR, ROC 7, RSI 14, EMA 50, and Bollinger Bands.  
LSTM with Fundamental Indicators (LSTM FM): This model focuses on fundamental economic indicators such as GDP, inflation rates, interest rates, and trade balances to forecast forex price movements.

LSTM with Technical and Fundamental Indicators (LSTM TM FM): This comprehen- sive model combines technical and fundamental indicators, providing a holistic view of the market dynamics influencing forex prices.

LSTM with Technical, Fundamental, and Sentiment Analysis (LSTM TM FM SA): This configuration integrates technical and fundamental indicators with sentiment scores de- rived from financial news headlines. This model captures the immediate impact of market sentiment on forex prices within shorter intervals, aiming to enhance predictive accuracy by leveraging real-time market sentiment. Each configuration was tested on the respective datasets for the four key forex pairs (EUR/USD, NZD/USD, EUR/NZD, and AUD/NZD). The perfor- mance of these models was assessed using a comprehensive suite of metrics, including MAE, MAPE, RMSE, R², and the Spearman correlation coefficient. These metrics provided a quanti- tative assessment of the model’s accuracy and the value added by integrating sentiment analysis with technical and fundamental indicators.

2. **XGBoost**

The XGBoost model was implemented to leverage its robust gradient-boosting framework, which effectively handles structured data and captures complex patterns. The model’s capabil- ity to handle large datasets and its flexibility in tuning parameters made it an ideal choice for this research. The XGBoost models were trained and evaluated using both One-day and Four- hour OHLC data, combined with technical indicators (TM), fundamental indicators (FM), and sentiment analysis (SA) scores.

To prepare the data for the XGBoost model, it was essential to standardise the features and targets to ensure that all features had a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one. This standardisation was performed using the StandardScaler from the sklearn library. Standardising the data helps achieve stable and efficient training of the XGBoost model by ensuring that the features are on a comparable scale.

The data was split into training and test sets using an 80-20 split, ensuring that 20% of the data was reserved for testing. This split was performed using the train test split function from sklearn, with the shuffle parameter set to False to maintain the time series order of the data. The target variable (CLOSE price) was also scaled to ensure consistent scaling across all features.

The XGBoost model was constructed using the XGBRegressor from the XGBoost li- brary, with the objective function set to reg:squarederror, which is suitable for regression tasks. A comprehensive hyperparameter tuning process was undertaken using GridSearchCV to identify the optimal hyperparameters for the model. The hyperparameter grid included a

range of values for max depth, learning rate, n estimators, subsample, colsample bytree, gamma, and reg lambda. The GridSearchCV approach involved performing an exhaustive search over specified parameter values for the XGBoost estimator. This search was evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation to ensure robustness and generalisability of the results. The scor-

ing metric used was neg mean squared error, which minimises the squared error between the predicted and actual values.

The training process for the XGBoost model involved fitting the model on the scaled training data and validating it using cross-validation to prevent overfitting. The best hyperpa- rameters identified from the grid search were used to fit the final model, ensuring that the model was optimised for predictive performance.

The XGBoost model’s architecture included the following key parameters:

* **Max Depth:** This parameter controls the maximum depth of the trees. A higher value can increase the model’s capacity to learn complex patterns but may also lead to overfitting.

* **Learning Rate:** This parameter determines the step size at each iteration while moving toward a minimum of the loss function. A lower learning rate requires more trees but can improve the model’s performance.

* **Number of Estimators:** This parameter defines the number of boosting rounds. More rounds can lead to better performance but may also increase the risk of overfitting.

* **Subsample:** This parameter controls the sample fraction to fit the individual base learn- ers. Subsampling can prevent overfitting by introducing randomness.

* **Colsample bytree:** This parameter controls the fraction of features used for fitting each tree. Similar to the subsample, it helps reduce overfitting by adding randomness.

* **Gamma:** This parameter specifies the minimum loss reduction required to partition a leaf node further. A higher value leads to more conservative algorithms.

* **Reg lambda:** This parameter adds a regularisation term to the loss function, which helps in preventing overfitting.

These parameters were fine-tuned to optimise the performance of the XGBoost model, ensur- ing that it effectively captured the underlying patterns in the forex data.

3. **Ensemble Model**

The ensemble model was developed to combine the strengths of LSTM and XGBoost models, aiming to improve predictive accuracy by leveraging the unique capabilities of each model. The ensemble approach involved training LSTM and XGBoost models separately and then combining their predictions using a weighted averaging technique.  
![][image26]

Figure 11: Architecture of the Ensemble Model Combining LSTM and XGBoost.

The LSTM model was trained using standardised One-day and Four-hour OHLC data and technical, fundamental, and sentiment indicators. The preprocessing steps involved stan- dardising the features and targets using the StandardScaler from the sklearn library, ensur- ing that all features had a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one. The data was structured into sequences using a time step, capturing temporal dependencies effectively.

The XGBoost model was trained on the same standardised data, using a comprehensive hyperparameter tuning process with GridSearchCV to identify the optimal hyperparameters. The best hyperparameters were used to fit the final XGBoost model, ensuring it was optimised for predictive performance.

Once both models were trained, their predictions were combined using a weighted av- eraging technique. The weights were determined based on the performance of each model, with the LSTM model generally receiving a higher weight due to its superior performance in capturing temporal patterns. The ensemble model’s predictions were then evaluated using a comprehensive suite of metrics, including MAE, MAPE, RMSE, R², and the Spearman corre- lation coefficient.

As shown in Figure [11,](#figure-11:-architecture-of-the-ensemble-model-combining-lstm-and-xgboost.) the detailed architecture of the ensemble model combines LSTM and XGBoost. The ensemble model’s architecture included the following steps:

* **Training LSTM and XGBoost Models:** Both models were trained separately using standardised data and optimised hyperparameters.

* **Making Predictions:** Each model made predictions on the test data, which were stan- dardised to ensure consistency.

* **Combining Predictions:** The predictions from both models were combined using a weighted averaging technique, with weights assigned based on each model’s perfor- mance.

* **Evaluating Performance:** The ensemble model’s predictions were evaluated using a comprehensive suite of metrics to assess its predictive accuracy and the value added by combining LSTM and XGBoost models.

By integrating the strengths of LSTM and XGBoost models, the ensemble model aimed to provide more accurate and robust forex price predictions, leveraging the temporal patterns captured by LSTM and the complex patterns identified by XGBoost.

4. **Transformer Model(TRANSFORMER EN DE)**

The Transformer model captured complex dependencies within sequential forex data, lever- aging its architecture’s strengths in handling long-range dependencies and parallel process- ing capabilities. The Transformer model used in this research included encoder and decoder components designed to process historical forex data and predict future price movements. To prepare the data for the Transformer model, preprocessing steps involved standardising the fea- tures and targets to ensure all features had a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one. This standardisation was performed using the StandardScaler from the sklearn library. Standar- dising the data is crucial for achieving stable and efficient training of the Transformer model by ensuring that the features are on a comparable scale.  
The data was structured into sequences using a sequence length of 10, aligning with the chosen temporal resolution for the Transformer model. This involved creating sliding windows of data to capture temporal dependencies effectively. Each window consisted of ten consecutive

time steps of input features, with the target being the forex price at the subsequent time step. The Transformer model was constructed using the TensorFlow Keras library, with an architec- ture that included both encoder and decoder layers. The encoder processed the input sequences, capturing dependencies within the data. The decoder used these processed sequences to predict future prices, considering the historical context provided by the encoder.

The architecture of the Transformer model included several key components:

* **Transformer Block:** Each block consisted of a multi-head attention mechanism, fol- lowed by a feed-forward network. Multi-head attention allowed the model to focus on different parts of the input sequence simultaneously, capturing various aspects of the temporal dependencies. Layer normalisation and dropout were applied to improve gen- eralisation and stability.

  * **Encoder:** The encoder comprises multiple Transformer blocks, processing the input se- quences to extract meaningful representations. Each block in the encoder included multi- head attention and feed-forward layers.

    * **Decoder:** The decoder also comprised multiple Transformer blocks, with each block fo- cusing on the encoder outputs and the previous decoder outputs. The decoder’s attention mechanism allowed it to focus on relevant parts of the encoder’s output while generating predictions.

      * **Output Layer:** A time-distributed dense layer was used as the final output layer, apply- ing a linear activation function to predict the forex price at each time step.

L2 regularisation was applied to all dense layers to prevent overfitting, which penalises large weights and encourages the model to learn simpler patterns. The Adam optimiser was employed with an initial learning rate, and learning rate scheduling was implemented using the ReduceLROnPlateau callback. This callback reduced the learning rate by 0.5 when the validation loss plateaued, ensuring that the model continued learning even when improvements slowed. Early stopping was also employed using the EarlyStopping callback, which monitored the validation loss and stopped training if there was no improvement for 60 epochs, restoring the best weights observed during training. The training process for the Transformer model involved fitting the model on the training data and validating it using validation data to mon- itor the model’s performance and prevent overfitting. The model was trained for up to 1000 epochs with a batch size tailored to the dataset. The performance of the Transformer model was assessed using a comprehensive suite of metrics, including MAE, MAPE, RMSE, R², and the Spearman correlation coefficient. These metrics provided a quantitative assessment of the model’s accuracy and the value added by integrating sentiment analysis with technical and fun- damental indicators.

5. **Transformer Model(TRANSFORMER DE)**

The Transformer Decoder model captured complex dependencies within sequential forex data, leveraging its architecture’s strengths in handling long-range dependencies and parallel pro- cessing capabilities. This research utilised a Transformer model with a decoder-only architec- ture to process historical forex data and predict future price movements.

Figure 12: Decoder Architecture of the Transformer Model.

To prepare the data for the Transformer model, preprocessing steps involved standardis- ing the features and targets to ensure all features had a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one. This standardisation was performed using the StandardScaler from the sklearn library. Standardising the data is crucial for achieving stable and efficient training of the Transformer model by ensuring that the features are on a comparable scale. The data was structured into sequences using a sequence length of 8, aligning with the chosen temporal resolution for the Transformer model. This involved creating sliding windows of data to capture temporal depen- dencies effectively. Each window consisted of eight consecutive time steps of input features, with the target being the forex price at the subsequent time step.  
The architecture of the Transformer model included several key components, as illus- trated in Figure [12:](#figure-12:-decoder-architecture-of-the-transformer-model.)

* **Transformer Block:** Each block consisted of a multi-head attention mechanism with a look-ahead mask, followed by a feed-forward network. Multi-head attention allowed the model to focus on different parts of the input sequence simultaneously, capturing various aspects of the temporal dependencies. Layer normalisation and dropout were applied to improve generalisation and stability.

  * **Decoder:** The decoder is comprised of multiple transformer blocks. Each block focused on the decoder’s attention mechanism, allowing it to concentrate on relevant parts of the input sequence while generating predictions.

    * **Output Layer:** A time-distributed dense layer was used as the final output layer, apply- ing a linear activation function to predict the forex price at each time step.

  The model’s architecture included the following layers:

      * **Input Layer:** Accepting the standardised input sequences.

      * **Transformer Blocks:** Processing the input sequences through multiple layers containing multi-head attention and feed-forward layers.

      * **Output Layer:** A dense layer with a linear activation function that produces the final price predictions.

The look-ahead mask was used in the attention mechanism to ensure that the model could only attend to previous and current positions in the sequence, preventing it from using future information during training. This is crucial for time-series forecasting tasks, which aim to predict future values based on past and current observations. The look-ahead mask cre- ates a triangular matrix that masks out future time steps, allowing the model to maintain the autoregressive property necessary for sequential data prediction.

L2 regularisation was applied to all dense layers to prevent overfitting, which penalises large weights and encourages the model to learn simpler patterns. The Adam optimiser was employed with an initial learning rate, and learning rate scheduling was implemented using the ReduceLROnPlateau callback. This callback reduced the learning rate by a factor of 0.5 when the validation loss plateaued, ensuring that the model continued to learn even when improve- ments slowed down. Early stopping was also employed using the EarlyStopping callback, which monitored the validation loss and stopped training if there was no improvement for 60 epochs, restoring the best weights observed during training. The training process for the Trans- former model involved fitting the model on the training data and validating it using validation data to monitor the model’s performance and prevent overfitting. The model was trained for up to 1000 epochs with a batch size tailored to the dataset.
